Part E · Chapter 4

Vision-language models

How the parts of a vision-language model are joined, how many tokens a photo takes, and where a small model's answers go wrong

A vision-language model (VLM) joins a vision encoder to a language model, with a projector that puts image tokens in the prompt (LLaVA) or with cross-attention layers (Flamingo). This chapter follows one photo through Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct, covers two training stages, counts its tokens, probes failures and sketches test-time adaptation, my project at MBZUAI. The answers come from one small model on a few photos. Photos are credited under the figures.

You will need: patches and image tokens (E1), encoders (E2), cross-attention (E3), the generation loop and the KV cache (D5), prompts and templates (D7) and murky water (C3).

From photo to answer

Guess first. You send SharkCam a photo of a hammerhead, 640 by 362 pixels, with the question "Which shark is this, and is it protected?" The question has 10 tokens. Will the photo take fewer tokens than the question, about as many or many more? Which half of the question can the photo answer?

A vision-language model (VLM) is a language model that can also read photos. Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct, the model of this page, is one and has three main parts in a row. A vision encoder turns the photo, cut into patches (blocks of 16 by 16 pixels), into one vector per patch (a list of numbers, whose width is how many numbers it has). A projector turns these vectors into image tokens, which have the width of the language model's word vectors. The language model reads the image tokens together with the question and writes the answer.

  1. Press Next step until the line under the cards reads "Step 4 of 6". Card 2 shows 22 × 40 = 880 patches, and card 4 turns them into 220 image tokens.
  2. Press Next step. Card 5 shows the prompt, the tokens read before the model writes, as 220 image tokens (navy), 10 question tokens (coral) and 10 template tokens (sand).
  3. Press Next step for the answer and, under the cards, a check of its claims.

About the model and the numbers

The model is Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct. Its vision tower has 24 blocks of width 1,024 and 406,957,056 numbers. Its language model has 28 layers of width 2,048 and 1,720,574,976 numbers, of which 311,164,928 are the table of word vectors. The numbers of tokens are counted from the prompt that the processor builds. The mean lengths of the vectors and the answer are measured on this photo. The answer is shown as the model wrote it, with its Markdown marks (the asterisks are bold type). The question is the same for all photos, so the answers differ only because of the photo and the model.

The hammerhead photo takes 220 image tokens and the question 10, so the photo takes 22 times as many tokens as the question.

How it works

Follow the hammerhead photo. The processor (the code that prepares the photo) resizes it so that both sides are multiples of 32 pixels, the side of 2 patches (640 by 362 becomes 640 by 352). Cutting it into patches of 16 by 16 pixels gives 352 / 16 = 22 rows and 640 / 16 = 40 columns, so 880 patches. The vision encoder gives one vector of 1,024 numbers per patch. The projector joins blocks of 2 by 2 patches, so four vectors become one of 4 × 1,024 = 4,096 numbers. Two layers (next section) map that vector to 2,048 numbers, the width of the language model, and 880 / 4 = 220 image tokens come out.

The prompt is all the tokens that the language model reads before it writes. It has the image tokens, the 10 tokens of the question and 10 template tokens, which are fixed tokens that mark the parts of the prompt.

this photo:220image tokens, Nimg+10question tokens, nq+10template tokens, ntpl=240prompt tokens, n

Common belief. A correct shark name means that the model's other claims about that shark can be trusted.

Why it fails. For the hammerhead photo the answer says "hammerhead shark", which is right. It then gives the IUCN category (a rating of extinction risk) as Vulnerable, although the IUCN lists the scalloped hammerhead of the photo as Critically Endangered. It also names a US law about marine mammals, which does not cover sharks. A photo can show a shark and cannot show a rating or a law, so a correct name does not check those claims.

Better account. Split the question. Ask the model what the photo shows, and check the claims about protection against a source.

Quick quiz

A photo of 1,024 by 768 pixels goes to this model. How many image tokens does it take?

The sides 1,024 and 768 are multiples of 32 (32 × 32 and 32 × 24), so there is no resize. An image token covers 2 by 2 patches, which is 32 by 32 pixels, so the tokens are 32 × 24 = 768.

Which half of the question can the photo answer, and what does the other half need?

The first half, because the shark is in the photo. Whether it is protected depends on what a law or a list says, which a photo does not show. The other half needs a source, such as a table of species and statuses kept by people.

About the model and the answers

All answers on this page are the output of Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct (Alibaba Cloud, Apache-2.0), run offline in 32-bit floating point with greedy decoding unless the text says otherwise. Greedy decoding always writes the most probable next token (D3), so repeating the run on the same machine gives the same answer. The answers were copied into data files. A model with 2 billion numbers is small, and the tests use a handful of photos, so the results describe these runs only. They are no benchmark. Examples written for this page are labelled.

A second photo and the cache

The bamboo shark photo is 640 by 480, so both sides are already multiples of 32 and the grid is 30 by 40 patches. Joining 2 by 2 gives 15 by 20 = 300 image tokens, and the prompt has 320 tokens. The photo takes 30 times as many tokens as the question. The spadenose photo takes 260 image tokens and the milk shark photo 300. For the hammerhead photo the model wrote 196 tokens.

While it writes, the model uses the key-value cache of D5, which stores the keys and values of the tokens already read. The cache takes 114,688 bytes per token (28 layers, 8 key and value heads of 128 numbers, keys and values, 16 bits). The prompt of 320 tokens alone takes 320 × 114,688 = 36.7 MB. The prompt of the first photo takes 240 × 114,688 = 27.5 MB.

Symbols

\[ n = N_{\text{img}} + n_{\text{q}} + n_{\text{tpl}},\qquad \text{cache} = 2\,N_{\text{layer}}\,n_{\text{kv}}\,d_{\text{head}}\,b\;n \]

  • \(N_{\text{img}}\) is the number of image tokens, \(n_{\text{q}}\) the tokens of the question and \(n_{\text{tpl}}\) the special tokens of the template. Their sum \(n\) is the prompt length.
  • \(N_{\text{layer}}\) is the number of layers (28), \(n_{\text{kv}}\) the number of key and value heads (8) and \(d_{\text{head}}\) the numbers per head (128). \(b\) is the bytes per number (2 at 16 bits). The factor 2 counts keys and values. This is the cache formula of D5, with the sizes of this model.

What the answer got right and wrong

The question has two halves. "Which shark is this" can be answered from the photo. "Is it protected" cannot, because a photo does not show what a law says, so a model with no tool or source can answer it only from the text it was trained on. The model answered both halves from the same numbers. For the hammerhead photo it said "hammerhead shark", which is right. It also named the great hammerhead, a different species from the scalloped hammerhead in the photo. It gave the IUCN category as Vulnerable, and the IUCN lists both species as Critically Endangered. It named two US laws. NOAA Fisheries lists four populations of the scalloped hammerhead under the Endangered Species Act, so that claim is partly right for the shark in the photo. US laws do not set what is allowed in Indian waters. The Marine Mammal Protection Act covers marine mammals, and sharks are fish, so that claim is wrong. The wrong claims in this fluent answer are hallucinations (D7): fluent claims that the photo or the model's training does not support.

Two meanings of protected

"Protected" has more than one meaning. A species can be rated threatened by the IUCN, which is a statement about the risk of extinction. It can be on a schedule of a national law, which is a statement about what people may do. For India, two ICAR-CMFRI posters on the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022, give two cases. I checked both entries in the Gazette text of the Act (Act 18 of 2022). The Ganges shark is on Schedule I (poster 65 of 2024). The scalloped hammerhead is in Appendix II of Schedule IV, the list of species whose international trade is regulated (poster 69 of 2025). The great hammerhead that the model named is on Schedule II, so for these two species a wrong name also gives a wrong schedule. Schedules change, so check the current schedule before you rely on this. The design that follows for SharkCam is simple. Let the VLM read the photo, and answer the second half from a table of species and statuses kept by people, called as a tool (D7).

Common mistakes

Debug tip. When answers sound plausible and ignore the photo, count the image tokens in the prompt. The count should equal (H′ / 32) × (W′ / 32) for the resized photo. A prompt with no image tokens, or with a photo that was resized to a few tokens, can give fluent answers that come from the question alone. Also try a plain grey picture: asked "Which shark is this?" with a grey picture, this model answers "great white", and no shark in the picture can have caused that answer.

More questions

The resized hammerhead photo (640 by 352) has 3 colour values per pixel. How does their number compare with the numbers in the 220 image tokens of 2,048 numbers?

The photo has 640 × 352 × 3 = 675,840 colour values. The image tokens contain 220 × 2,048 = 450,560 numbers, two thirds as many.

Two ways to give a model eyes

Guess first. A language model reads tokens, and a photo is not made of tokens. Name two ways to let the model use a photo: change the photo into something the model reads, or change the model. Which of the two makes the prompt longer, and which adds layers?

In the LLaVA design, a projector turns the patch vectors of the vision encoder into image tokens. These join the prompt, the tokens the language model reads, so the prompt grows with the number of image tokens. In the Flamingo design the prompt keeps only text tokens, so the photo adds no image tokens to it. A resampler reduces the patch vectors to 64 visual tokens (vectors outside the prompt), and new cross-attention layers between the layers of the language model read them. The words supply the queries, and the 64 visual tokens supply the keys and values.

  1. Press Next step until the line under the diagrams begins "Step 3". On the left the image tokens (navy) and text tokens (coral) form one sequence. On the right the text stays alone, and an arrow from "64 tokens" runs into the teal cross-attention boxes.
  2. Press Next step once more. The labels show what learns and what is frozen (not updated in training). On the right only the resampler and the cross-attention layers learn.

LLaVA-style: image tokens in the prompt

Flamingo-style: cross-attention layers

The LLaVA design adds image tokens to the prompt and no layers; the Flamingo design adds cross-attention layers and no prompt tokens.

How it works

Take the projector of the hammerhead photo. The vision encoder gives 880 patch vectors, so joining 2 by 2 blocks gives 220 rows. A table of numbers is written as rows × columns, so this one is 220 × 4,096: 220 rows of 4,096 numbers. The projector multiplies it by a first matrix (a 4,096 × 4,096 table, so the product has 220 rows again). It then applies GELU, a fixed function, to the numbers separately and multiplies by a second matrix. In the line below, the × between tables is this product.

this model:220 × 4,0962 by 2 patches joined×4,096 × 4,096first layer→ GELU ×4,096 × 2,048second layer=220 × 2,048image tokens

A layer from m numbers to k numbers has m × k matrix entries and k biases (one added number per output). The first layer here has 4,096 × 4,096 + 4,096 = 16,781,312 learned numbers, and the second has 8,390,656. Add a layer norm (a rescaling step, 2 × 1,024 = 2,048 numbers) and the projector has 25,174,016 learned numbers, 1.2% of the model's 2,127,532,032.

Common belief. The projector translates the photo into words that the language model reads.

Why it fails. For the hammerhead photo, an image token and its nearest word vector typically have a cosine similarity of 0.094 (1 means the same direction, 0 means unrelated). A random direction typically has 0.095 with its nearest word vector, and a word has 0.59 with its nearest neighbour word. So for this photo the image tokens are no closer to words than random directions are.

Better account. The projector is a learned code, and its vectors work for the language model after training, like a new kind of token.

Quick quiz

A photo gives 220 image tokens and the question has 10. How long is the prompt, ignoring template tokens, in the LLaVA and Flamingo designs?

It has 220 + 10 = 230 tokens in the LLaVA style, because the image tokens join the prompt. It has 10 tokens in the Flamingo style: the prompt keeps only the words, and the cross-attention layers read the 64 visual tokens.

A layer maps a vector of 512 numbers to a vector of 2,048 numbers and adds a bias per output. How many learned numbers does it have?

The count is 512 × 2,048 + 2,048 = 1,048,576 + 2,048 = 1,050,624.

The two designs in the papers

LLaVA (Liu and others, 2023) uses the vision encoder of CLIP (E2) and a language model. One trainable matrix connects them. It maps a patch vector to a vector of the language model's width. LLaVA-1.5 (Liu and others, 2024) replaced the matrix with a two-layer MLP and raised the photo to 336 pixels, which gives 24 × 24 = 576 image tokens. Qwen3-VL, the model of this page, belongs to the same family. Its projector joins 2 by 2 patches first and then applies two layers. Its configuration also lists three extra projectors, and the technical report (Bai and others, 2025) describes DeepStack as combining features from several levels of the vision transformer. I did not study that part.

Flamingo (Alayrac and others, 2022) takes the other route. A frozen vision encoder feeds a resampler that outputs 64 visual tokens for any photo or video. A frozen language model has new cross-attention blocks inserted between its original blocks, one block in four for the 9 billion parameter model. They are the cross-attention of E3, with queries from the text and keys and values from the 64 tokens. A new block is multiplied by tanh of a learned number that starts at 0, so that at the start of training the model is the original language model, unchanged. In the text of an interleaved prompt, a word attends to the photo that came just before it. It does not attend to earlier photos.

Symbols

\[ H_{\text{img}} = Z\,W + \mathbf{b},\qquad H_{\text{img}} = \mathrm{GELU}\!\left(Z\,W_1 + \mathbf{b}_1\right)W_2 + \mathbf{b}_2 \]

  • \(Z\) is the table of patch vectors from the encoder, one row per patch (or per joined block). \(H_{\text{img}}\) is the table of image tokens, one row per token, with the width of the language model. This is the matrix product of 0.5.
  • The first form is LLaVA's single matrix \(W\). The second is the two-layer form of LLaVA-1.5 and of Qwen3-VL's projector (GELU is the activation of B1).

A second worked example

The layer norm on the 1,024 numbers of a patch vector has a scale and a shift per number, 2 × 1,024 = 2,048 numbers. The total of 25,174,016 is the number that the model reports for its projector. A second case is LLaVA-1.5. Its patch vector has 1,024 numbers (the width of CLIP ViT-L). The same two-layer form maps 576 patches to 576 tokens. There is no joining, because a patch is one token.

In Python

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(4127)
Z = rng.normal(size=(22, 40, 1024))                  # patch vectors on a 22 x 40 grid (made-up numbers)
# join 2 x 2 neighbours: 4 patches become one vector of 4 x 1024 numbers
J = Z.reshape(11, 2, 20, 2, 1024).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3, 4).reshape(220, 4096)
W1 = rng.normal(size=(4096, 4096)) / 64; b1 = np.zeros(4096)
W2 = rng.normal(size=(4096, 2048)) / 64; b2 = np.zeros(2048)
gelu = lambda x: 0.5 * x * (1 + np.tanh(np.sqrt(2 / np.pi) * (x + 0.044715 * x ** 3)))
H = gelu(J @ W1 + b1) @ W2 + b2                      # image tokens for the language model
print(J.shape, H.shape)
print("numbers in the two layers:", W1.size + b1.size + W2.size + b2.size, "plus the layer norm:", 2 * 1024)
print(np.allclose(J[0], np.concatenate([Z[0, 0], Z[0, 1], Z[1, 0], Z[1, 1]])))   # the first token contains patches (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)
(220, 4096) (220, 2048)
numbers in the two layers: 25171968 plus the layer norm: 2048
True

Image tokens are not words

The number 0.094 in the box "Common belief" above is the median over the 220 image tokens of the hammerhead photo. The test also compared lengths. The mean length of an image token is 22.4, and a word vector has a mean length of 1.45. The LLaVA paper describes the first stage of training as making a visual tokeniser for the frozen language model.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If the code fails with a message about image features and image tokens that do not match, count them. The number of image placeholders in the text must equal the number of rows that the projector returns. A processor that was changed (a different maximum size, for example) while the model was not will show this error.

More questions

Why does a Flamingo block start with a factor of tanh(0) = 0?

The new block then adds no output at the start of training, so the model begins as the original language model. The cross-attention can then grow from zero, and the language ability of the frozen model is not disturbed at the start.

Align first, then instruction-tune

Guess first. The projector starts as random numbers, so its image tokens have no meaning for the language model yet. Suppose you trained the whole model on questions about photos from the first step. What could go wrong with the language model? Which parts would you train first, and on what data?

A part learns when training changes its numbers, and a frozen part is not changed. LLaVA is trained in two stages, and its vision encoder is frozen in both. In stage 1, alignment, only the projector learns, on photos with short captions, and the language model is frozen too. In stage 2, visual instruction tuning, the projector and the language model learn together, on questions and answers about photos. The loss counts only some tokens: the caption in stage 1 and the answer in stage 2.

  1. Choose Stage 1: align. Only the Connector learns (here the projector and three extra projectors, 4.7% of the numbers; the projector alone is 1.2%), and the loss counts the 12 tokens of a made-up caption (teal) of 252.
  2. Choose Stage 2: instruction-tune. The language model learns too, so 85.6% of the numbers move, and the loss counts the 196 answer tokens of 436.
  3. Switch to LLaVA-1.5 and choose both stages in turn: stage 1 has 558,000 caption pairs, stage 2 has 665,000 examples.

One training example of this stage, drawn with the token counts of the hammerhead photo (the caption of stage 1 is a made-up example of 12 tokens)

Data sizes: LLaVA (Liu and others, 2023) and LLaVA-1.5 (Liu and others, 2024). The sizes of the three parts are those of Qwen3-VL-2B, counted from the model, with the LLaVA recipe applied as an illustration. Qwen's own recipe is longer and is in its technical report. The connector here is the projector and the three extra projectors.

Stage 1 would train 4.7% of the numbers of this model and count the caption in the loss; stage 2 would train 85.6% and count the answer.

How it works

Follow the hammerhead example through stage 2. Its sequence has 220 image tokens, 20 question and template tokens and 196 answer tokens, 436 in all. The loss mask selects the tokens that count, here the 196 answer tokens, because the model must learn to write them. The loss of a token is −ln p, where p is the probability that the model gave to the correct next token and ln is the natural logarithm. A smaller p gives a larger loss. A token with p = 0.5 adds −ln 0.5 = 0.69 nats (the unit of this loss), and one with p = 0.1 adds 2.30. The loss L is the average over the counted tokens, a number that training tries to make small.

stage 2:0.69loss L, in nats=1 / 196one over the number of counted tokens×196 × 0.69sum of −ln p over the counted tokens, p = 0.5

With p = 0.5 for all counted tokens, the average is 0.69 for 196 answer tokens or for the 12 tokens of a caption. The image tokens add no term, but the answer tokens read them through attention, so the loss still depends on the projector.

Common belief. To teach a model to see, show it photos with questions from the first step.

Why it fails. At the start the projector's output has no meaning, so a full update could push the language model to fit noise and lose what it learned earlier. The LLaVA paper argues for this order, and this page has not run the comparison.

Better account. Train the new connection first with the old parts frozen, then release the language model.

Quick quiz

In stage 1 of LLaVA, which parts are frozen, and which part learns?

The vision encoder and the language model are frozen. Only the projector learns.

In stage 2 an answer has 100 tokens, and the correct token has probability 0.1 at all 100 positions. What is the loss, and how many of the 220 image tokens add a term?

A counted token adds −ln 0.1 = 2.30 nats, so the average over the 100 counted tokens is 2.30. No image token adds a term, because only the answer tokens count.

The recipes

In stage 1 the vision encoder and the language model are frozen, and only the projector changes. It is trained on image and caption pairs: 595,000 pairs in LLaVA, filtered from a public caption set, and 558,000 in LLaVA-1.5. A pair is turned into a request to describe the image briefly and the caption as the reply. In stage 2 the projector and the language model learn, on 158,000 conversations, descriptions and reasoning questions in LLaVA, and on 665,000 examples in LLaVA-1.5. The encoder stays frozen in both stages.

The LLaVA paper describes stage 1 as training a visual tokeniser for the frozen language model, and it argues the order as follows. If the projector were random and the language model free to change, the loss could push the language model to fit noise, and it could lose what it learned earlier (B7). The paper shows its results for the order. This page has not run the comparison.

Flamingo uses one stage on a large mix of web text, photos and video. The encoder and the language model are frozen, and only the resampler and the cross-attention blocks are trained. Its authors tested the tanh factor and the spacing of the blocks in ablations on a 3 billion number model. Removing the tanh factor lowered the overall score by 4.2 points (70.7 to 66.5). One block in four, instead of a block in all layers, made training 66% faster for a loss of 1.9 points, as the paper reports.

Symbols

\[ L = -\frac{1}{|A|}\sum_{t\in A}\ln p_\theta\!\left(y_t \mid \text{image},\ \text{question},\ y_{\lt t}\right) \]

  • \(A\) is the set of positions of the answer tokens (the loss mask of D7), \(y_t\) the token at position \(t\) and \(y_{\lt t}\) the answer tokens before it. \(p_\theta\) is the model's probability of a token (D3).
  • The image tokens, the question and the template are read but have no target, so they add no term to the sum. With the hammerhead example, the loss counts 196 of 436 tokens (45%) in stage 2, and 12 of 252 (4.8%) for a caption of 12 tokens in stage 1.

Where it breaks

A model trained only on short answers is likely to give short answers. The 665,000 examples of LLaVA-1.5 include short-answer questions as well as long conversations. The recipe is an illustration for a model of this size, and Qwen3-VL's own training has more stages.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a trained model ignores the photo, give it a plain grey picture and compare the answers. If they are the same as with the actual photo, the answers do not depend on the photo. The grey test is also a baseline for the questions on a test set.

More questions

The caption has 12 tokens and the image 220. How many tokens does the loss count in stage 1?

The 12 tokens of the caption. The image tokens and the request have no target and are not counted.

How many tokens a photo costs

Guess first. A processor with fixed resolution resizes all photos to one size, so they get the same number of image tokens. With dynamic resolution it keeps the photo's size, rounded to multiples of 32. A frame of the SharkCam dive is 640 by 362 pixels and a phone photo is 4000 by 3000. Under dynamic resolution, about how many times as many image tokens as the dive frame does the phone photo get: 5, 15 or 50?

In Qwen3-VL an image token covers 32 by 32 pixels (2 by 2 patches of 16 by 16). So the number of image tokens is about the photo's area divided by 32 × 32 = 1,024, within a minimum and a maximum area. This is dynamic resolution, so a larger photo gives more tokens. LLaVA-1.5 uses fixed resolution. Its Hugging Face processor scales the short side to 336 pixels and crops the middle 336 by 336. The photo is then cut into patches of 14 pixels, which gives 24 × 24 = 576 tokens for any photo.

  1. Press "Phone, 4000 × 3000". The coral diamond (your photo) rises to 11,750 image tokens, about 53 times the 220 of the dive frame, while the navy LLaVA-1.5 line stays at 576.
  2. Press "Thumbnail, 224 × 224". The result is 64 tokens, the least this processor gives: 224 × 224 / 1,024 is 49, but the processor enlarges photos smaller than 256 by 256.

Measured with the released processors of Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct (Apache-2.0), llava-hf/llava-1.5-7b-hf (licence listed as llama2), llava-hf/llava-v1.6-mistral-7b-hf (LLaVA-NeXT, Apache-2.0) and SmolVLM-256M-Instruct (Apache-2.0). The pictures were plain grey, since the count depends on the size only. The 4000 by 3000 point comes from the formula, and the Qwen3-VL processor gives the same 11,750 tokens.

For Qwen3-VL a 640 by 362 frame gives 220 image tokens and a 3840 by 2160 frame gives 8,160, while LLaVA-1.5 gives 576 for any photo.

How it works

Take the dive frame, 640 by 362 pixels. The processor (the code that prepares the photo) rounds both sides to multiples of 32. For the width, 640 / 32 = 20 tokens across. For the height, 362 / 32 = 11.3, which rounds to 11, so the resized height is 11 × 32 = 352 pixels and there are 11 tokens down. This gives 11 × 20 = 220 image tokens.

dive frame:640 × 362photo, W × H in pixels→640 × 352after the resize, W′ × H′÷32 →20 × 11tokens across and down=220image tokens, Nimg

In the figure a dive is 2,400 frames of 220 tokens, which is 528,000 image tokens. The model can read at most 262,144 tokens at once, so this dive does not fit in one prompt. The key-value cache stores the keys and values of the tokens already read, at 114,688 bytes per token with 16 bits. So a dive that did fit would need 528,000 × 114,688 bytes = 60.6 GB (decimal). The fold of the first section shows where 114,688 comes from. The function smart_resize under Go deeper applies the rule of this section.

Common belief. More tokens always mean a better answer.

Why it fails. More tokens cost time and cache memory, and they add detail only if the photo has it. A 112 by 112 thumbnail is enlarged to 256 by 256 and gets 64 tokens, yet the enlargement adds no detail.

Better account. Spend tokens where the detail is. A crop of the part of the photo that contains the information keeps its detail, and the model reads fewer tokens than for the whole photo.

Quick quiz

How many image tokens does an 800 by 600 photo give in Qwen3-VL?

The side 800 gives 800 / 32 = 25. The side 600 gives 600 / 32 = 18.75, which rounds to 19, so H′ = 608. The tokens are 19 × 25 = 475, as the processor returns.

A phone photo of 4000 by 3000 pixels has a tag 120 pixels tall. About how tall is the tag after the LLaVA-1.5 processor scales the short side to 336 pixels?

The processor scales the short side to 336 pixels and crops the middle 336 by 336, whatever the photo's size, and the 576 tokens cover only that square. The short side is 3,000, so the scale factor is 336 / 3,000 = 0.112, and the 120 pixel tag shrinks to about 120 × 0.112 = 13 pixels. Thin letters lose detail before the model reads anything.

How the processors count

Qwen3-VL cuts the photo into patches of 16 by 16 pixels and joins 2 by 2 patches into a token, so a token covers 32 by 32 pixels. The processor first rounds both sides to a multiple of 32, and halves go to the even multiple, as in Python's round. It then keeps the area between 65,536 pixels (256 by 256) and 16,777,216, the minimum and maximum pixels, which keep a tiny photo from giving too few tokens and a huge photo too many. A 112 by 112 thumbnail is enlarged to 256 by 256 and costs 64 tokens. A 1920 by 1080 frame is rounded to 1920 by 1088: 60 × 34 = 2,040 tokens. A 3840 by 2160 frame is rounded to 3840 by 2176: 120 × 68 = 8,160 tokens. The formula of this page agrees with the processor at all 11 sizes that were measured. The LLaVA-1.5 processor scales the short side of any photo to 336 pixels and crops the middle 336 by 336. It cuts that into patches of 14 pixels: 24 × 24 = 576, which is fixed. LLaVA-NeXT uses a variable number of tiles, and its processor returned 1,176 to 2,928 tokens in these measurements. The SmolVLM-256M processor returned 832 to 1,088. The cost of a fixed size is detail: a photo of a tag gets the same number of tokens as a photo of a landscape. The next section measures what a small token budget does to small text.

Symbols

\[ H' = 32\,\mathrm{round}\!\left(\tfrac{H}{32}\right),\quad W' = 32\,\mathrm{round}\!\left(\tfrac{W}{32}\right),\qquad N_{\text{img}} = \frac{H'}{32}\cdot\frac{W'}{32} \]

  • \(H, W\) are the height and width of the photo in pixels, \(H', W'\) the sizes after the resize (before the limits on the area), and \(N_{\text{img}}\) the number of image tokens. The 32 is the 16 pixels of a patch times the 2 patches joined on a side.
  • For a patch of side \(P\) and no joining this is the \(N = (S/P)^2\) of E1.

The dive and the levers

The practical levers on the cost of a dive are the maximum number of pixels in the processor, the number of frames (take one in ten), and a crop around the animal. All three give up some detail to save tokens. Compare the 528,000 tokens of the dive with the 470,400 patch tokens of D6, where a frame of 224 pixels gave 196 patches.

In Python

import math
def smart_resize(h, w, factor=32, min_pixels=65536, max_pixels=16777216):
    r = lambda x: max(factor, round(x / factor) * factor)      # Python's round: halves go to the even number
    hh, ww = r(h), r(w)
    if hh * ww > max_pixels:
        beta = math.sqrt(h * w / max_pixels)
        hh, ww = math.floor(h / beta / factor) * factor, math.floor(w / beta / factor) * factor
    elif hh * ww < min_pixels:
        beta = math.sqrt(min_pixels / (h * w))
        hh, ww = math.ceil(h * beta / factor) * factor, math.ceil(w * beta / factor) * factor
    return hh, ww
def image_tokens(w, h):
    hh, ww = smart_resize(h, w)
    return (hh // 32) * (ww // 32)
measured = {(112, 112): 64, (224, 224): 64, (336, 336): 100, (448, 448): 196, (640, 362): 220, (640, 480): 300,
            (800, 600): 475, (1024, 768): 768, (1280, 720): 880, (1920, 1080): 2040, (3840, 2160): 8160}
for (w, h), n in measured.items():
    print(w, h, image_tokens(w, h), n, image_tokens(w, h) == n)
print("dive:", 2400 * image_tokens(640, 362), "tokens;", round(2400 * image_tokens(640, 362) * 114688 / 1e9, 1), "GB of cache")
112 112 64 64 True
224 224 64 64 True
336 336 100 100 True
448 448 196 196 True
640 362 220 220 True
640 480 300 300 True
800 600 475 475 True
1024 768 768 768 True
1280 720 880 880 True
1920 1080 2040 2040 True
3840 2160 8160 8160 True
dive: 528000 tokens; 60.6 GB of cache

The second column is what the function computes and the third what the processor returned. The 336 pixel case shows why the halves go to the even number. The value 336 / 32 = 10.5 rounds to 10 in Python and to 11 in a plain rounding. The processor gives 100 tokens, which is 10 × 10.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a model runs out of memory on a high-resolution photo, print the number of image tokens first. Halving both sides of a large photo divides the tokens by about 4. A maximum number of pixels in the processor fixes the problem without touching the model.

More questions

How many image tokens does a 1280 by 720 frame give in Qwen3-VL?

The side 1280 gives 1280 / 32 = 40 and 720 gives 720 / 32 = 22.5, which rounds to 22 (the even number), so H′ = 704. The tokens are 22 × 40 = 880, as the processor returns.

Where it goes wrong

Guess first. Four things are known to trouble vision-language models: counting objects, reading small text, stating what is not in the photo, and handling photos unlike the training photos (such as murky water). For this 2 billion number model on shark photos, rank the four from the one you expect to fail first.

A probe is a small test built to find one kind of failure. The figure runs four probes on this model, Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct. In counting and in reading text it was right on easy versions and wrong on harder ones, so those probes have an edge, where the answers turn wrong. It did not name the species of any of the four shark photos, and murky water changed some names. Of 70 yes or no questions about what is in the photo, it answered 69 right.

  1. On Counting, drag the slider to 12 and then to 24 copies of a shark pasted on a white board (made up). Coral boxes mark wrong answers: 14 at 12 copies, and 16 and 30 at 24.
  2. On Small text, look at Letter size em 6 (em is the font size in pixels; the capital letters are 4 pixels tall): it reads the tag number 4127 as "4327". Press "Photo at twice the size" to get "4127", with 920 image tokens instead of 220.
  3. On Murky water, choose Bamboo shark, tank and drag Depth (a simple model) from 0 to 15 m. The answer changes from "banded shark" to "great white".

Copies of one shark pasted on a white board (a made-up composite picture; the model saw this picture)

Question: "How many sharks are in this image? Answer with one number." The shark is cut out of spadenose-1 (Hariprasad Shetty10, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons). Three random layouts per count; the picture shown is the first.

The tag as the model saw it (a made-up tag drawn on the hammerhead photo)

Question: "What number is on the tag? Answer with the number only." (or the weight, for the long tag). Photo: Kevin Lino, NOAA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. The text is made-up. "em" is the size of the font in pixels in a photo 640 pixels wide.

Eight answers to "Which shark is this? Answer with the common name only." (sampling, temperature 0.7)

What the model got right in the easy versions of the tests

Counting was right in all 18 pictures with 1 to 8 copies, and right in 3 of 9 with 12, 16 or 24 copies.

How it works

Two probes have an edge. At 12 copies (right answer 12) the model answered 14, 12 and 12 for three random layouts of the copies, at 16 copies 15 three times, and at 24 copies 16, 24 and 30. In a photo 640 pixels wide, the made-up tag "TAG 4127", drawn on the hammerhead photo, was read right at all seven sizes with capital letters 6 pixels tall or more. It was wrong at three of the five smaller sizes.

Species names were wrong or missing even in clear photos. The model was asked eight times per photo for a shark's common name (with random sampling, so answers can differ). For the hammerhead photo it gave the group name "hammerhead" in all eight answers. None of its 24 answers for the other three photos named the species. For the bamboo photo it said "banded shark" six times, although the photo shows a grey bamboo shark. In the figure's simple depth model (colour and contrast only), its answer for that photo changed to "great white" at 15 m.

Common belief. A model that answers well on easy tests will answer well on the field photos.

Why it fails. Easy versions lie before an edge (12 copies, capital letters below 6 pixels tall, 15 m of simulated murky water), and a field photo can lie beyond it.

Better account. Find the edge for your photos with a probe. Keep a check that needs no model (a table, a second view or a person), because a model can be consistently wrong.

Quick quiz

Six of eight answers for the bamboo shark photo are "banded shark". Does this show that the answer is right?

No. It shows that the model is fairly consistent, and a consistent answer can still be wrong: the photo shows a grey bamboo shark. Asking several times can reveal guessing. It cannot reveal a consistent mistake.

Why did the photo at twice the size read a tag that the photo at the normal size missed?

At twice the size the photo has 920 image tokens instead of 220, and the tag is drawn twice as large in pixels, so a letter covers more pixels and more tokens. A likely reason for the better reading is that more of the letter forms reaches the language model. This page did not test the cause.

Go deeper the probes in detail, descriptions, a debug tip about 6 min

Counting

On the natural photos (1 to 3 sharks, or none) the model gave the right number for all 11. To find the edge, the composites paste 1 to 24 copies of one shark on a white board. Up to 8 copies the count is right in 18 of 18 trials. From 12 copies it drifts: 14, 12, 12, then 15, 15, 15, then 16, 24, 30. This fits the finding of Rahmanzadehgervi and others (2024) that VLMs miss simple visual facts that people get right. They report an average of 58% for four models on seven simple tasks. The edge depends on the picture. Small copies, overlap and clutter are likely to lower it, and this page did not test them.

Small text

The tag says "TAG 4127" and the photo is 640 pixels wide. The size of the letters is given in em, the size of the font in pixels in a photo 640 pixels wide. At its own size, the answers for letter sizes em 3 to 7 (capital letters 2 to 5 pixels tall) are "10", "1014127", "4127", "4327" and "4127". That is two clear misses, one wrong digit and two right. From em 8 up (capital letters 6 pixels tall), all seven sizes were read right. At twice the size (920 tokens instead of 220) the only miss is the smallest tag, which read "4327". On the longer tag with several numbers the question asked for the weight. The weight "0.281" was read right at four of five sizes at 1× and came back as "283" at the smallest size. At 2× it was right at all five sizes. A token covers 32 by 32 pixels, and a letter 3 pixels tall is a small part of it. A likely reason for the wrong answers is that too little of the letter forms reaches the model, which then writes a plausible number. This page did not test the cause. Spending more tokens helped here, which is the trade of the section on cost.

Names and facts

Sampling chooses the next token at random in proportion to its probability (D3), here with a temperature of 0.7, so answers differ from run to run. Asked for the common name of the shark 8 times with sampling, the model said "hammerhead" 8 times for the hammerhead photo. For the grey bamboo shark it said "banded shark" 6 times, "dusky shark" once and "dogfish" once. For the spadenose shark it gave 7 different names in 8 tries, and for the milk shark 6. None of the 24 answers for these three photos names the species of the photo. A consistent answer ("banded shark" six times) can be wrong, and scattered answers suggest a guess. Asking several times and comparing is a cheap check. It finds guessing and cannot find a consistent mistake.

In two-sentence descriptions of all 14 photos, the model named the objects correctly in my reading: clownfish in an anemone, an eagle ray, a dolphin, two grey sharks on rock. For the spadenose shark, the two drawings of the Ganges shark, the milk sharks at a market and the turtle, the species names that it gave were wrong. It called the spadenose shark "Squalus acanthias (commonly known as the blacktip shark)". The photo shows a spadenose shark, so both names are wrong. It called the Ganges shark drawing "Carcharhinus (Pseudodon) gansettius", a name I could not match to a species. The olive ridley turtle became a "green sea turtle". A yes or no test had 70 questions: is there a diver, a dolphin, a turtle, a ruler or a shark in the photo? Of these, 69 were right. The one miss was a shark that the model called absent. Three questions had a false premise. Asked "What colour is the diver's wetsuit?" on the hammerhead photo, it refused. Asked "What name is written on the tag?" on the bamboo shark photo, it said that there was no tag. Asked how many people are next to the turtle, it said one person was in the background, which matches a small figure far away in the photo. So the hallucinations that appeared were claims about names and laws, as in the first section. Li and others (2023) found object hallucination to be common in large vision-language models. It was worse for objects that are frequent in the instruction data or that often appear together with the objects in the photo. A photo with a reef and a diver in the water would probably be a harder test than mine.

Murky water

At 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 and 30 m of the simple depth model of C3, the answer for the hammerhead photo stays "hammerhead". For the bamboo shark photo "banded shark" becomes "great white" from 15 m. For the spadenose photo it goes blacktip, banded, banded, barracuda, barracuda, great white. The 18 pictures made from the three shark photos (3 photos at 6 depths) all got "yes" to "Is there a shark in this photo?". The 16 pictures without a shark all got "no". They are the turtle, dolphin, clownfish and ray at 0, 10, 20 and 30 m. So this model had no false alarms on 16 pictures. The ResNet-18 of C3 and the CLIP model of E2 gave growing shark scores on the same kind of photos. The questions differ (a yes or no answer here, a score there), and 16 pictures are a small test. The species names changed with depth for two of the three shark photos. Depth only changes colour and contrast in that model, and an actual change of water would also change the animals and the angle.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Keep a fixed set of probe photos, with sizes, counts and depths close to those of the photos that SharkCam takes, and run them after any change of model, processor or prompt. Record the answers as well as a pass or fail. A change from "banded shark" to "great white" at a depth of 15 m is visible in the answers and may be invisible in a score.

Adapting at test time

Guess first. In the murky-water probe the species names changed for two of the three shark photos. The model has 2.1 billion numbers, and nobody labels the frames of a dive. Which part of the model would you let change while it reads the dive, and what could serve as the target?

Test-time adaptation changes a model a little while it is used, without labels. In the design of this section, a small set of numbers, the fast weights, may change while the model reads. They start again from the trained values for the next input. After a chunk (a block of tokens) is read, an update changes them by an amount computed from a self-made target. The target is built from the chunk itself, so no label is needed (the fold shows how). Which numbers, and how often, are design choices.

  1. With the chip "Fast weights: 5 down-projections" chosen (one matrix in the MLP of a block, defined below), read the first box under the strip: 62,914,560 numbers may change, 2.96% of the model.
  2. Drag Chunk size down to 512 tokens. The coral marks on the strip, the ends of chunks, move closer together, and the updates over 2,400 frames rise from 128 to 1,031.
  3. Choose the last chip. All 2,127,532,032 numbers may change, as in ordinary training.

Frames of a dive, murkier along the way (the hammerhead photo through the depth model). Coral marks: the end of a chunk, where an update would happen.

Sizes are counted from Qwen3-VL-2B. The choice of five blocks (0, 6, 12, 18 and 24) applies the stride of the text-model study of D6 to a 28-block model as an illustration. No project made this choice. One frame is 220 tokens, as for a photo of 640 by 362 pixels.

Five down projections are 62,914,560 numbers (2.96% of the model), and a dive of 2,400 frames gives 128 updates. The figure shows counts from the design and no results.

How it works

Take the default choice, five down projections. The MLP of a transformer block is the part that works on one token at a time. It ends with a down projection, here a matrix of 6,144 × 2,048 = 12,582,912 numbers. Blocks 0, 6, 12, 18 and 24 of the 28 (one block in six, chosen as an illustration) give 5 × 12,582,912 = 62,914,560 numbers. That is 62,914,560 / 2,127,532,032 = 2.96% of the model. In this design only these numbers may change, so the others keep their trained values. A chunk of 4,096 tokens contains 4,096 / 220 = 18.6 frames of 220 tokens, and a dive of 2,400 frames is 528,000 tokens.

dive:2,400 × 220frames times tokens per frame = 528,000 tokens÷4,096tokens per chunk=128.9chunks→128updates, one per complete chunk

Common belief. Test-time adaptation means retraining the model on new data after it is deployed.

Why it fails. In this design there are no labels, and only 2.96% of the numbers can change. They go back to the trained values for the next input, so the model is not retrained.

Better account. It is a small update during use, with a target made from the input, and it can move the model the wrong way. So run a no-shift check first. On clear-water frames the answers with the update on and off should be the same.

Quick quiz

If you let the down projections of ten blocks change, what share of the model is that?

Ten blocks have 10 × 12,582,912 = 125,829,120 numbers, and 125,829,120 / 2,127,532,032 = 5.91%.

With chunks of 4,096 tokens and frames of 220 tokens, how many updates does a dive of 1,000 frames give?

The dive has 1,000 × 220 = 220,000 tokens, and 220,000 / 4,096 = 53.7, so there are 53 complete chunks and 53 updates.

Go deeper what can change, the update, my project about 3 min

What can change

The domain-shift chapter (C3) re-estimated the statistics of batch normalisation on new frames, one way to adapt. This model has no such stored statistics to re-estimate: it uses layer norm or RMS norm, which compute their statistics per token (B6). The options in the figure are the other choices. The scale numbers of the norm layers are 248,832 numbers in all. The projector has 100,714,496 with its three extra ones. The fast weights of D6 are the down projections of some MLP blocks (D5). This model has 12,582,912 numbers in the down projection of a block, and five blocks if one block in six is chosen. The whole language model has 1,720,574,976. The two sliders change the chunk size and the length of the dive. The strip shows where the updates fall, and the frames get murkier from left to right, as in the stream of C3.

The update

In the text-model version of the method, an update happens after a chunk is read. It adds to the fast weight an outer product of a target made from the chunk's own tokens and the layer's hidden vectors, so no label is needed. The fast weights go back to the trained values for the next input (D6). In a VLM the chunk contains image tokens as well as words. A chunk of 4,096 tokens is about 18.6 frames at 220 tokens, so a dive of 2,400 frames gives 128 updates. A question that decides the design is whether the target built from murky frames points in a useful direction. This page has no data on that question. The update can move the model the wrong way: in C3, re-estimating the statistics of a network on a pool of 14 photos made its shark confidence worse.

Bridge to my project. In-Place Test-Time Training, a method from ByteDance Seed (Feng and others), treats the down projection of selected MLP blocks as fast weights. It updates them chunk by chunk as the model reads, with a target built from the input. Generation never pauses: an update happens in the step that completes a chunk. At MBZUAI, in Prof. Salman Khan's group, I am porting the method from text models to a Qwen vision-language model, so that it can adapt to an input after deployment. My motivation is the failure of this section: recognising a shark when the water, light and animals change between dives. See the project page and its primer. This page reports no result of the project. The figure above shows sizes and counts only.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Run the no-shift check of C3 first. On clear-water frames, the answers with the update on and off should be the same. If they differ, the update itself is doing damage, and the murky-water result cannot be trusted.

More questions

Why can the batch-norm trick of the domain-shift chapter not be copied directly to a VLM?

A transformer uses layer norm or RMS norm, which take their statistics from one token, so there are no stored averages over a batch to replace by new ones.

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory A photo is 1000 by 800 pixels. Find the sides after the resize, the number of patches of 16 by 16 and the number of image tokens in Qwen3-VL. Then find the length of the prompt for a 12 token question with 10 template tokens, and the key-value cache of the prompt at 16 bits (114,688 bytes per token).

    Hint

    1000 / 32 = 31.25 and 800 / 32 = 25. The number of patches is the number of tokens times 4.

  2. theory The projector of LLaVA-1.5 for 576 patches of 1,024 numbers is a two-layer MLP with a hidden width of 4,096 and an output width of 4,096. Count its numbers with biases, and compare with the 25,174,016 of the Qwen3-VL projector. Explain the difference in terms of the inputs.

  3. theory In stage 1 the loss counts a caption of 12 tokens. Suppose the model gives the true token a probability of 0.25 on average. Find the loss. Then find the number of image tokens that would add to the loss, and say why.

  4. theory Compare a design with image tokens in the prompt and a design with cross-attention (E3). Name one cost that is lower for the first and one that is lower for the second, using the counts of this chapter and of E3.

Practice

  1. practice Use smart_resize from the code block. Find photo sizes for which the number of tokens is 1,024, with sides that are multiples of 32. Find as many as you can. Then find the largest 16:9 photo (width and height as multiples of 32) that stays under 1,000 tokens.

  2. practice Open data/vlm2.json of this chapter (https://mailab.in/primer/e4-vlms/data/vlm2.json). For the field count, compute the mean absolute error of the model's counts for all N, and plot it. Say at which N it first exceeds 0.5.

  3. practice Write a function chunks(frames, tokens_per_frame, chunk) that returns the number of updates and the frame at which an update happens for a dive. Check it for 2,400 frames, 220 tokens per frame and chunks of 4,096 (128 updates, the first at frame 19).

Think deeper

  1. open SharkCam must tell a fisher whether a shark is protected. Design the system. Which part is the VLM, and which part is a table? Who keeps the table up to date? What does the robot say when the VLM's name is not in the table?

  2. open You have 200 labelled dive frames and want to know whether a VLM is safe to use at depths of 15 m and more. Design the test: the questions, the number of runs per frame, the measures (accuracy, consistency, false alarms), and the result that would make you say no.

  3. open A test-time update on murky frames might help or hurt. Design an experiment with a no-shift check, a murky set and a control that updates on random frames. Say what you would conclude if the control improves as much as the update itself.

Come back later

Answer after two days and again after a week, without looking back.

Name the two designs for joining a vision encoder to a language model, and say what they do with the photo's patch vectors.

LLaVA style: a projector maps the vectors to the width of the language model, and they enter the prompt as image tokens. Flamingo style: a resampler makes 64 tokens, and cross-attention layers inserted in the frozen language model read them (designs).

E3 showed that BLIP's cross-attention puts about three quarters of its weight on a few empty patches. What would you expect for the weights of the language model on image tokens in a LLaVA-style model, and how would you test it?

The same kind of parking is possible, since a softmax row must add up to 1 and the model has a first token to park on (D6). A test is to measure the weight of the answer tokens on the image tokens, and the value lengths, as in E3.

C3 and D6 both leave most of a model fixed during test-time adaptation. What does the figure of this chapter say about how much is allowed to change, and what must be checked first?

About 3.0% of the numbers, in the figure's main option. The no-shift check on clear frames must come first, to show the update does no harm when no shift has happened (C3, adapt).
